messages.content: You are an acceptance reviewer. Answer only in the requested schema, and answer only the question the instructions ask.

You are de-duplicating a set of obligations derived from the software requirements in one task file.

You are given PAIRS of obligations. For each pair, answer one question: do these two obligations state exactly the same requirement?

Most pairs will not, and "no" is the right answer for most of them. You are not choosing the best partner for anything and you are not searching for duplicates.

**The test for sameness, and the only one that matters.** Two obligations state the exact same requirement if and only if BOTH hold:

1. They have identical truth conditions. They are true under exactly the same conditions and false under exactly the same conditions. If you can describe any delivered change that satisfies one and not the other, they are different requirements.
2. The exact same set of tests would demonstrate both. Not two tests in the same file, and not two assertions about the same function — the SAME test, asserting the same thing.

Apply that test explicitly before reporting any pair.

Note that sameness is transitive: if A and B are the same requirement, and B and C are the same requirement, then A and C are the same requirement. If you are unsure, do not link them.

Similar wording, a shared subject, or belonging to the same feature are not evidence of sameness; only the two conditions above are.

Cases that pass the test:
- The same demanded behavior stated in different words.
- A requirement and a clause giving the REASON for that requirement. The reason is not separately checkable, so no test can distinguish them.

Cases that FAIL the test, and are the common mistakes:
- A behavior and the technology used to implement it. "The amount is written with two decimal places" and "the file is produced with the standard CSV library" can each hold while the other fails, and no single test shows both.
- A general requirement and a specific case of it. The specific case can pass while the general one fails.
- Two requirements about the same area of the change that demand different things.
- Obligations sharing vocabulary but not the demand.

**When you are unsure, do not link them.** Leaving two obligations separate costs a little redundancy. Linking two obligations that demand different things destroys one of the requirements, and nothing downstream can recover it. Prefer the redundancy.

Answer every pair you are given. Answering `false` for all of them is a valid and common outcome.

Answer for every pair below. Each is independent.

[pair-0000]
  A: [export-invoices-to-csv] from requirement task-01
    description: The system exports invoices to a CSV file, writing invoice data as CSV-formatted rows into a file.
    observable behavior: Running the export produces a CSV file that contains the invoices' data as comma-separated rows.
  B: [csv-header-row-names-every-column] from requirement constraint-01
    description: The export writes a header row naming every column.
    observable behavior: The first row of the exported CSV file is a header row whose fields name every column present in the data rows.

[pair-0001]
  A: [csv-header-row-names-every-column] from requirement constraint-01
    description: The export writes a header row naming every column.
    observable behavior: The first row of the exported CSV file is a header row whose fields name every column present in the data rows.
  B: [one-row-per-invoice] from requirement constraint-02
    description: The export writes exactly one data row per invoice, so the number of invoices can be counted from the row count without parsing any amounts.
    observable behavior: Exporting N invoices produces N data rows (excluding the header), one row per invoice, with no invoice split across multiple rows and no multiple invoices merged into one row.

  A: [one-row-per-invoice] from requirement constraint-02

    observable behavior: Exporting N invoices produces N data rows (excluding the header), one row per invoice, with no invoice split across multiple rows and no multiple invoices merged into one row.
  B: [export-escapes-customer-name-commas] from requirement constraint-03
    description: The export escapes embedded commas in the customer name so that a customer name containing a comma is written as a single field and does not split into extra columns.
    observable behavior: An invoice whose customer name contains a comma appears in the exported CSV as a single customer-name field, and the row parses back to the same number of columns as every other row with the original name intact.

    observable behavior: An invoice whose customer name contains a comma appears in the exported CSV as a single customer-name field, and the row parses back to the same number of columns as every other row with the original name intact.
  B: [amount-two-decimal-places] from requirement constraint-04
    description: The amount column of the exported CSV is written with exactly two decimal places for every invoice row, including whole-number amounts (e.g. 12 is written as 12.00) and amounts with a single decimal digit (e.g. 12.5 is written as 12.50).
    observable behavior: Each data row's amount field in the CSV output matches the pattern of digits, a decimal point, and exactly two digits.

    observable behavior: Each data row's amount field in the CSV output matches the pattern of digits, a decimal point, and exactly two digits.
  B: [csv-uses-stdlib-csv-module] from requirement constraint-05
    description: The CSV export file is produced using Python's standard-library csv module (e.g. csv.writer or csv.DictWriter) rather than hand-rolled string formatting or a third-party library.
    observable behavior: The export code imports and uses the standard-library csv module to write the file's rows, with no third-party CSV library or manual comma-joining of fields.
